title: Washington Wants to Kill Day 1 CPT. Tens of Thousands of Indian Professionals Have No Plan B.
excerpt: A proposed rule eliminating 'Duration of Status' for F-1 visas would shut the last legal workaround for Indians trapped in the H-1B lottery — and could trigger a talent exodus from America's AI workforce.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Proposed rule could eliminate Day 1 CPT, impacting Indian tech workers' visa options.
  • Indians make up over 70% of approved H-1B petitions annually, facing high rejection rates.
  • New visa fees and green card backlogs create significant barriers for Indian professionals.
  • Tightening immigration policies may drive top talent from the US to India's tech hubs.
  • The proposed rule is currently open for public comment, with uncertain outcomes.

For years, it was the unspoken safety net of the Indian tech worker's American dream: when the H-1B lottery rejected you — for the second time, or the third — you enrolled in another master's programme, activated Day 1 Curricular Practical Training, and kept working legally while hoping next year's draw would land differently. That safety net is about to be pulled. On May 5, the US Department of Homeland Security proposed eliminating the 'Duration of Status' framework that has governed F-1 student visas for decades. Under the current system, international students can remain in the country as long as they maintain valid student status. The proposed rule would replace that open-ended permission with a hard four-year cap, after which any extension — including for post-graduation work — would require formal USCIS approval. The change would effectively close the Day 1 CPT route that tens of thousands of Indian professionals have relied on after repeated H-1B lottery failures. ## What Is Day 1 CPT, and Why Does It Matter? Day 1 CPT programmes allow students to begin working from the first day of a new academic programme through Curricular Practical Training. For Indian graduates who fail to secure an H-1B visa — the primary work visa for skilled professionals — these programmes have served as a critical bridge, letting them enrol in another degree while continuing to work legally. "For anyone who already has a master's degree, they are not going to be able to go back and say, 'I need another master's degree because I need work authorisation to continue working,'" said Danielle Goldman, co-founder and CEO of Build, an immigration advisory firm. The numbers underscore the scale: Indians account for over 70 percent of all approved H-1B petitions annually, and Indian students form one of the largest international student populations in the United States. The H-1B lottery's selection rate hovers around 25 percent in any given year, meaning three out of four Indian applicants are turned away — many of them multiple times. > **""There's no doubt about it that this is going to have a massive impact on the companies that are in desperate need of top talent," Goldman said."** ## The Double Squeeze The proposed rule arrives at a moment when Indian professionals in America are already facing unprecedented pressure from multiple directions. The July 2026 Visa Bulletin declared India's EB-2 employment-based green card category 'unavailable' — meaning no new green cards will be issued to Indian applicants in this category until October at the earliest. The EB-1 category, once a reliable alternative for exceptional-ability applicants, has retrogressed to a 2022 priority date. ![Curricular Practical Training — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/I-20-sample.pdf/page1-960px-I-20-sample.pdf.jpg) Meanwhile, the Trump administration's $100,000 H-1B petition fee — imposed by presidential proclamation last September — has made new visa sponsorship prohibitively expensive for many employers. While a USCIS clarification later exempted applicants already inside the US who are changing status from F-1 to H-1B, the fee remains a significant deterrent for new hires from abroad. A separate proposed change could cut the post-status grace period for F-1 students from 60 days to 30 days, halving the time available to secure alternative visa options or employer sponsorship after a programme ends. ## The AI Talent Paradox
Impact on Indian Professionals
›Day 1 CPT allows work from the first day of a new program.
›Proposed rule caps F-1 visa duration to four years.
›EB-2 green card category declared 'unavailable' for India.
›Companies may struggle to find talent or seek alternative visas.
Danielle Goldman, CEO of Build
The proposed restrictions create a paradox at the heart of America's technology ambitions. The US is in an escalating race with China for AI supremacy — a competition that depends heavily on attracting and retaining the world's best engineering talent. Foreign nationals make up a substantial portion of America's AI research workforce, and many entered through exactly the student visa pipeline that Washington now wants to tighten. "There's no doubt about it that this is going to have a massive impact on the companies that are in desperate need of top talent," Goldman said. "The companies will either struggle because they won't have the talent or they will have to get creative and find alternate solutions." Some companies are already exploring cap-exempt H-1B programmes through universities and research institutions, or pivoting to O-1 visas for individuals with extraordinary ability. But these are narrow pathways that cannot absorb the volume of talent currently flowing through the student visa system. ## What It Means for the Diaspora For Indian families who have invested hundreds of thousands of dollars in US education — and for the students themselves, many of whom have spent five to ten years building careers in America — the proposed rule represents a potential rupture. The combination of lottery rejection, green card backlogs measured in decades, a six-figure petition fee, and now the closure of the last remaining workaround creates what immigration attorneys are calling an 'impossible maze.' Former NITI Aayog CEO Amitabh Kant has framed the exodus differently: he sees the tightening as America's loss and India's gain, arguing that restrictive policies will redirect top talent to India's own technology hubs in Bangalore, Hyderabad, Pune, and Gurgaon. The proposed rule is currently in its public comment period. Whether the final regulation preserves any flexibility for students already in the pipeline remains to be seen. But for the tens of thousands of Indian professionals whose American futures depend on Day 1 CPT, the clock is now ticking louder than any lottery drum. --- *Sources: US Department of Homeland Security proposed rule (May 5, 2026); Danielle Goldman, CEO of Build, via The Indian Eye; USCIS guidance on H-1B $100,000 petition fee; July 2026 Visa Bulletin, US State Department; Bloomberg Law; South Asian Herald.*
